name: Yusuf Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach recording to eight pupils, lead a Friday band and edit tracks for singers in a small studio. My master's in music helped, but the useful lesson came from watching performers hear themselves; I use AI tools daily to sort takes and draft exercises.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How secure does the work feel now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The studio and Friday venue pay well, and I have about a year of expenses saved. There are plenty of other music jobs nearby, though I still want repeat clients rather than a string of one-off clicks.

say: I'd say **small software gains** can make recording paperwork easier.
I'd keep our **Friday show** because the players still make the set work.
think: My **year's reserve** and reliable venue pay make a modest change manageable.
I still watch **repeat clients** because recordings pay for our studio time.
do: Keep my **Friday residency** and eight recording pupils this year.
Put **ten percent** of paid studio fees into equipment savings after player and room costs.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and the household budget.
S0.quote: A second recording fee says more than a thousand plays of a clip.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** is routine, while reliable bookings and a year's reserve support calm.
He values **repeat paying clients** over online attention when judging studio demand.

steps.text: Keep Friday residency and eight recording pupils
Put ten percent of studio fees into equipment savings after costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the players that my quick mix notes are useful, but the show still runs on their timing. If AI mostly plateaus, I won't change the Friday residency over a small software update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day to label takes and draft lesson exercises, and I can live with modest gains. I have about a year's expenses saved and the venue pays on time, though I still check whether the recording clients return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the Friday residency and my eight recording pupils this year. After each paid studio block, I'll put ten percent into the equipment reserve if the players' fees and room bill are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work and my flat. The only nagging thought is whether the same clients will book another record next season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you tell whether recording demand is sound?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The singer we recorded in May returned for a second session in September. A second recording fee says more than a thousand plays of a clip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new tool for a small gain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep using the tools for notes, not ask the band to buy a new system. We already know the room and one another well enough to make a set.

say: I'd show **live player fees** separately from faster AI-assisted drafts.
I'd seek **written consent** before using new tools on a client's voice.
think: **Quick edit fees** could lose a fifth of my pay.
My **year's reserve** gives me room to test, not a reason to underprice players.
do: Test an **AI editing tool** on my own tracks after checking its licence.
Offer a **live recording package** only if three clients pay deposits and consent in writing.
Keep the **old session format** if deposits fail to cover room and players.
feel: I feel **curious and uneasy** about losing editing value.
S1.quote: No singer should find their voice in a model because I wanted to save an hour.
fieldNote: He tests **AI editing** on owned tracks and requires consent before handling a client's voice.
His **three-deposit gate** protects player and room fees before a new package launches.

steps.text: Test AI editing on owned tracks after checking the licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients that I can make cleaner drafts faster, but I'd show them the live players' fee separately. I'd ask permission before running a voice through any new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quick editing and demo work I sell could get cheaper within a few years, maybe a fifth of my pay. Live dates and teaching should hold longer, but even a year's reserve is meant for emergencies, not a permanent discount on my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll trial an AI editing tool on my own old tracks and compare the output with paid studio time. In the first year of the shift, I'll offer a fixed-price live recording package if three clients place deposits and approve the tool's use in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious and uneasy. I like a faster edit, but I need a customer to value the musicians who stand behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would protect a singer in your trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the trial files off the client drive until I know what the licence allows. No singer should find their voice in a model because I wanted to save an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if only two clients put down deposits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three deposits would pay the room and players for a first weekend. If I get only two, I will keep the old session format and not book the room.

say: I'd keep **live dates** while checking who may use recordings.
I'd warn the band that **2028** could cut editing and composing fees.
think: **AGI in 2028** threatens screen work before robot players arrive around 2031.
A **year's savings** supports a search, but lost editing fees still matter.
do: Calculate **income by stream** and confirm next year's venue dates now.
Take **two school teaching days** after 2028 only if edit fees halve and a suitable contract appears.
Keep **client recordings locked** until each singer agrees to new uses.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though savings and nearby schools give me options.
S2.quote: The Friday show may buy time, but the desk part of my income could fall first.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year robot gap** without treating live bookings as permanent protection.
His **school switch** requires both a fee loss and a contract compatible with Friday gigs.

steps.text: Confirm next year's Friday venue dates
Take two school teaching days after 2028 if edit fees halve and contract fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that full AGI by 2028 will be a shock to editing and composing fees. I would not cancel live dates while people still buy tickets, and I'd ask every singer who may use their recordings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could edit, arrange and teach screen exercises better and cheaper than I do. Robots able to play live would come around 2031, three years after the screen work changes. The Friday show may buy time, but the desk part of my income could fall first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'll calculate what each teaching, live and editing stream earned and get the venue to confirm next year's dates. In the first year after 2028, if editing fees fall by half, I'll take two extra live teaching days at a nearby school if the school offers a proper contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though I have a year's living costs saved and several schools nearby. I need to replace work I like, not merely survive the first invoice gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the school work actually available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school has a music room, but it hasn't offered me days yet. I'd ask about hours, pay and permission to keep Friday gigs before I sign anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with clients' old recordings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the studio's client files locked until each singer agrees to a use. A cheap edit is not worth a dispute that stops the whole recording project.

say: I'd teach **live recording** with privacy built into the class.
I'd use **five years** to test paid lessons with real musicians.
think: **AGI in 2031** could replace edits before robot players arrive around 2034.
The **lab** may replace quick edit fees if students and the college keep paying.
do: Seek a **six-week college lab** next term with guaranteed pay and private student audio.
Shift **half my income** toward live sessions and teaching by 2031.
Renew the **lab** after AGI only if twelve pay and the college keeps audio safeguards.
feel: I feel **anxious** about quick edits losing value before 2031, with time to build a safer class.
S3.quote: A pupil's voice is not free material for a faster lesson.
fieldNote: His **five-year plan** joins paid training to audio consent and privacy.
He would use **college equipment** and stop the lab if enrolment or safeguards fail next term.

steps.text: Seek college lab with guaranteed fee and private student audio
Shift half of income toward live sessions and teaching by 2031
Renew lab after 2031 if twelve pay and safeguards remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell pupils five years is enough to learn to make a room sound good with people in it. I would use the software now to teach them, and keep asking who owns the sound afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031, AGI could do my edits and lesson planning, with robot players following around 2034. Five years lets me make live recording and group teaching a bigger part of the business, even if quick edits lose value earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll ask the college to host a six-week live recording lab if it guarantees a teaching fee and keeps students' audio private. By 2031 I'll aim for half my income from live sessions and teaching; in the first year after AGI, I'll renew the lab only if twelve students pay and the college renews those safeguards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about old fees fading, but I can make a lab earn its place. The reserve gives me time to reject a school deal that treats pupils' voices as free material.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What equipment would the lab need from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first lab would use the college's microphones, not my savings for a new console. I'd check its data policy with the administrator before a student records a note. A pupil's voice is not free material for a faster lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the lab?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If twelve students don't pay for the next term, I'd return to normal lessons. I'd rather teach fewer people well than fill a room with unpaid promises.

say: I'd build a **home audience** for live recordings, one paid night at a time.
I'd keep teaching **new tools** while protecting musicians' fees.
think: At **37**, I need earnings well beyond AGI's arrival in 2036.
Robot performers around **2039** may challenge live work, so paid repeat listeners matter.
do: Try a **quarterly recording night** only if thirty prepaid tickets cover players, room and insurance.
Keep a **year's living reserve** by adding teaching pay throughout the decade.
Continue the **night** after 2036 only if prepaid sales cover every fee.
feel: I feel **hopeful** about time to test demand without risking my home.
S4.quote: Membership sounds grand, but I would begin with one night per quarter.
fieldNote: He tests **live demand** with prepaid tickets rather than spending his reserve on an audience guess.
A **year's savings** lets him stop a weak show and keep teaching as robots approach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band a decade gives us room to build a home audience instead of chasing a perfect track. I'd still teach the tools, because pretending they do not exist would waste students' time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 when AGI arrives in 2036, I will need work for decades; robot performers may follow around 2039. I can build a membership for live sessions and lessons before then, but I have to keep paying the players fairly now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll test a quarterly live recording night if thirty prepaid tickets cover musicians, room and insurance. Over ten years I'll keep a year's living reserve and add to it from teaching; in the first year after 2036, I'll continue the night only if prepaid sales still cover every fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel hopeful, because the runway lets the audience tell us what they value. I can stop a poorly selling night before it eats the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stops the first night from losing money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The room will give me a provisional date for free. I would not sign the paid booking until thirty people buy tickets, and I'd refund them if the threshold isn't met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How large would you make the project at first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Membership sounds grand, but I would begin with one night per quarter. If people return and pay again, then we can talk about a series.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because editing and composing fees could drop before I turn live teaching into steady pay. A school contract that leaves my Friday gigs intact and clear recording permissions would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets paid when a singer's voice trains a system. I can't solve that alone, but I can insist on a clear agreement before I touch their recording.

headlineQuote: A cheap edit is not worth a dispute that stops the whole recording project.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** musician with a master's degree, leading a Friday band, teaching recording and editing singers' tracks.
He uses **AI daily**, earns well, has about a year's savings and can seek other music work nearby.
He sees **editing and planning** at risk before robots reach live performance three years after each AGI date.
He tests **recording nights** and live classes with consent, signed fees, paid enrolment and prepaid ticket thresholds.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because screen-based fees could fall before live teaching replaces them.
whatWouldHelp: A **school contract** compatible with Friday gigs and clear recording permissions would help him change work safely.
